interview_metadata.name: Thomas Gatlin
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: Okay um, I'm Thomas and I'm nine. I was born here in Texas and we live in Royse City. My mom said I was a really quiet baby and I just liked to look at stuff a lot. When I was little like four or five, I started drawing on everything, even the wall once, and my mom got kinda mad but then she taped a big roll of paper to the wall instead so I could draw there. I went to pre-K at the church place and then kindergarten at my school, and now I'm finishing fourth grade. My teacher Mrs. Halverson is really nice and she lets me draw in the margins if I finish my math early. The biggest things in my life are probably my family — my mom and dad and my little sister Ellie — and my friends from school and soccer. I play on the Oakwood Rangers and we had a tournament last fall where I scored one goal, which was huge. We went to the Grand Canyon two summers ago and that was the farthest I've ever been from home. Oh and last year my grandpa got really sick and we drove to see him in Tyler, that was kinda scary. I read a lot of graphic novels, like the Amulet series is my favorite. I want to be a comic book artist when I grow up, or maybe an engineer who makes cool gadgets.

follow_ups.question: You mentioned your little sister Ellie — how old is she and what's she like?
follow_ups.response: She's five. She's loud, like really loud, and she always wants to play with my LEGOs and break them. But she's funny too. She does this thing where she pretends to be a cat and meows at dinner and my dad laughs every time even though my mom says not to encourage her.

follow_ups.question: What happened when your grandpa got sick — is he doing better now?
follow_ups.response: He had something with his heart, I don't really know the word. They put a thing in there to help it. He's better now, he came over for Easter and he ate two pieces of ham. But my mom still calls him every Sunday to check.

follow_ups.question: What about the goal you scored — can you tell me about that moment?
follow_ups.response: It was the second game of the tournament and I was playing wing, and Caleb passed it to me kinda by accident I think, and I just kicked it and it went in the corner. Everyone screamed and my dad was on his feet. I drew a comic about it later, like I made myself the hero and it had a giant boot.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: Hmm. I'm only nine so I haven't had like a huge crossroad but maybe in second grade. There was this thing where I could either do art club after school or do the soccer skills clinic, and they were on the same day. I really wanted to do both. I cried about it kinda. My mom said I had to pick one for the season. I picked art club because I was nervous about soccer back then, I wasn't very good at it. But then the next year I tried soccer too and now I do both because they switched the schedule. I think if I'd just picked soccer first I might've stopped drawing as much, and drawing is like my favorite thing.

follow_ups.question: What made art club feel like the safer choice back then?
follow_ups.response: Because I already knew I liked drawing and I knew Mrs. Patel who runs it. Soccer was with a bunch of kids I didn't know and a coach who yelled, well not yelled mean, but loud. I was scared I'd mess up.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever wish you'd picked differently?
follow_ups.response: Not really. I like that I do both now. Mom says I got the best of it.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: I think I chose it, but my mom helped me choose. Like she asked me which one would make me sadder to miss, and I said art club, so that's how I picked. So sorta both — I chose but with help.

follow_ups.question: Does your mom usually help you decide things like that?
follow_ups.response: Yeah, she asks me questions until I figure out what I actually want. Dad just tells me what he thinks, which is sometimes faster but kinda less fun.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: I guess the school could have, like if they hadn't put them on the same day. That would've helped a lot. Or maybe if Mrs. Patel had been there to tell me art was fun even just on weekends or something. But it worked out okay.

follow_ups.question: Did anyone besides your mom give you advice?
follow_ups.response: My friend Jacob said do soccer because then we'd be on the same team. But I didn't, sorry Jacob.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I'm nine, so no partner or kids, that's a grown-up thing. My family is my mom Sarah, my dad Mike, and my little sister Ellie. My mom is a nurse, she works at the clinic in Rockwall and sometimes she has weekend shifts. My dad works in like, building stuff for houses, he's a contractor. Then there's Grandma and Grandpa Gatlin who live in Tyler, that's like two hours away, and my Grandma Joan on my mom's side lives in Greenville which is closer. I see Grandma Joan a lot, like every other weekend usually. She makes really good biscuits. My Uncle Pete is my dad's brother and he lives in Dallas with my Aunt Kim and they have a baby named Wyatt. We see them at Thanksgiving and stuff. Family is really important, my mom says family is the most important thing besides God.

follow_ups.question: What do you usually do with Grandma Joan when you visit?
follow_ups.response: We bake stuff, like cookies and one time a pie that kinda burned. She has a garden and she lets me dig in the dirt and find bugs. She also has cable TV with old cartoons so I watch those while she does her crossword.

follow_ups.question: How is your relationship with Ellie when she's not breaking your LEGOs?
follow_ups.response: She's okay. We share a bathroom which is annoying but we have a fort in the playroom we made together with blankets and we play 'restaurant' in there. I'm always the chef and she's always the customer who is mad about the food.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: Um, we have a dog named Biscuit, he's a brown mutt my dad got from the shelter. He counts as family. And my mom's sister Aunt Lacey but she lives in Houston so I only see her like twice a year.

follow_ups.question: Tell me about Biscuit.
follow_ups.response: He's like seven and he sleeps on my bed even though he's not supposed to. He's really chill. He doesn't bark much except at the mailman.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: My best friend is Jacob Mendez, he's been my friend since first grade. He lives like four streets over and his mom drives us to soccer together. Then there's Caleb who is on my soccer team and we hang out at recess. And there's Aanya from art club, she's really good at drawing horses, way better than me. Mrs. Halverson my teacher I already said. Coach Davis is my soccer coach and he's nice. And Mrs. Patel runs art club. Oh and Pastor Tim from church, he tells funny stories.

follow_ups.question: What do you and Jacob do when you hang out?
follow_ups.response: Mostly Minecraft. We have a server with just us two and we built a whole castle and a pretend mall. We also ride bikes sometimes around the neighborhood and we have a 'club' which is just sitting in the tree in his backyard.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see Jacob outside of soccer and school?
follow_ups.response: Like every weekend pretty much, either he comes over or I go there. Saturdays usually. Sometimes Friday after school we get pizza together.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: We live in Royse City which is in Texas, like east of Dallas. Our neighborhood has a lot of new-ish houses, like they were built when I was a baby my dad says. The streets are all named after trees, we live on Pecan Drive. There's a park at the end of our street with a playground and a basketball court, and there's a pond a little further with ducks. There's a Brookshire's grocery store and a Sonic and a Dollar General nearby. It's pretty quiet most of the time. Lots of kids though, like there's at least five kids my age on my street, and we sometimes do bike races or capture the flag in the summer.

follow_ups.question: What's your favorite thing about the park at the end of your street?
follow_ups.response: There's a really tall slide that I used to be scared of and now I'm not. And there's a big oak tree where my friends and I climb. Once I saw a hawk eat a lizard there which was kinda gross but cool.

follow_ups.question: How long has your family lived in this neighborhood?
follow_ups.response: Since before I was born. My mom said they bought the house when she was pregnant with me. So like ten years.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel safe. We don't lock our front door always. My mom does at night but during the day it's open if we're home. I can ride my bike to Jacob's by myself now which is new this year.

follow_ups.question: Has anything ever made you feel unsafe?
follow_ups.response: There was a coyote in someone's yard one time and everyone was warned to keep their cats inside. That was a little scary. And once a stranger knocked on the door selling stuff and my mom said don't open it.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: It's mostly good. The down part is it's kinda far from cool stuff like the big museums in Dallas, we have to drive a long time. And in the summer it gets really really hot like over 100. But there's tons of space and we have a big backyard and lots of friends nearby.

follow_ups.question: What do you do when it's that hot outside?
follow_ups.response: Either stay inside with the AC and do LEGO or Minecraft, or we go to the community pool, or sometimes my mom takes us to the library because it's cold in there.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: It's just me, my mom Sarah, my dad Mike, and my sister Ellie. And Biscuit the dog. Nobody else lives with us. Sometimes my Grandma Joan stays over for a weekend if my parents go away for a wedding or something but that's not most of the time.

follow_ups.question: Does Grandma Joan stay over often?
follow_ups.response: Like maybe three or four times a year. Last time was in March I think when my parents went to a wedding in Austin.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everyone permanent. Just us four and the dog.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: Just Grandma Joan sometimes. Oh and Jacob has slept over before like for a sleepover but that's not staying staying.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, everyone's here.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: Weekdays I wake up at like 7, eat cereal or sometimes eggs my dad makes, brush teeth, then mom drops me at school by 8. School is until 3:15. Mondays and Wednesdays I have art club after school until 4:30. Tuesdays and Thursdays I have soccer practice from 5 to 6:30 at the fields by the middle school. Fridays I usually just come home and chill. On weekends, Saturday morning is soccer games during the season, then we hang out, do errands with mom maybe, hang with Jacob. Sundays we go to church at 10 then have a big lunch at Grandma Joan's or our house, then I do homework and pack my bag for the week.

follow_ups.question: What church do you go to?
follow_ups.response: First Baptist in Royse City. We've been going since forever. Pastor Tim runs it. There's a kids' service after the main one called Sunday School and I usually go to that.

follow_ups.question: What's a typical Saturday game day like?
follow_ups.response: We get up early, like 7:30, and I put on my soccer kit which is blue and white. Mom packs orange slices and a sports drink. We drive to wherever the game is, sometimes Greenville or Wylie. Game's an hour. Then we get McDonald's or Whataburger after, that's our tradition.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I don't have a job, I'm a kid. But I have chores. I have to feed Biscuit in the morning and after school. I make my bed, mostly. I take out the recycling on Wednesdays. And I help unload the dishwasher when mom asks. I get five dollars a week allowance if I do everything. Some weeks I forget the recycling and then I only get four. I'm saving up for a LEGO Bionicle set that's like eighty dollars.

follow_ups.question: How long have you been saving for the LEGO set?
follow_ups.response: Since like Christmas, so five months. I have $47 in my jar. My mom said maybe she'll match what I save for my birthday in August.

follow_ups.question: What's the hardest chore?
follow_ups.response: Honestly the recycling because I always forget it's Wednesday. Mom puts a sticky note on the fridge now.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I help with Ellie sometimes, like reading to her at bedtime if mom is busy. And I'm supposed to practice piano fifteen minutes a day which I don't always do. I take piano lessons on Thursday mornings at school during the elective time. I also have to do reading log every night, twenty minutes, and write what book I read. I do that during dinner sometimes which is technically cheating maybe.

follow_ups.question: What book are you reading right now?
follow_ups.response: I'm rereading the third Amulet book because I love it. And for school we're doing 'Because of Winn-Dixie' which is okay, kinda slow but the dog is cute.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: The piano lessons started in February which is new. And I started being able to ride my bike to Jacob's alone, that started in March. Oh and my mom got a new shift schedule at the clinic so now she does Saturdays sometimes which means dad takes me to the soccer game which is fine but he doesn't pack the snacks as good.

follow_ups.question: How do you feel about your mom working Saturdays?
follow_ups.response: I don't love it. But it's only like twice a month. She makes up for it with extra movie nights on Friday.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: I don't have kids, I am a kid. I'm nine.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: Not really. We had Officer Friendly come to our school in second grade and he showed us his badge and stuff. And my dad got pulled over once on the highway, I was in the car, and the cop just gave him a warning about a tail light. That's about it.

follow_ups.question: What did you think about Officer Friendly's visit?
follow_ups.response: It was cool. He had a K-9 dog with him named Rex. We all wanted to pet him but you couldn't because he was working.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: Um, just seeing them at the State Fair maybe, doing security. And there's a sheriff who comes to our church sometimes who's a member there.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: Nope. Nobody I know.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I can't vote, I'm nine. My parents vote I think. My mom takes me with her sometimes to the polling place which is at the elementary school gym and I get a sticker.

follow_ups.question: What do you remember about going to the polls with mom?
follow_ups.response: It's like a regular day, you wait in line, she goes into a little booth. There's people with clipboards. The sticker is the best part, it says 'I Voted' and I put it on my backpack.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I don't really have political views, I think those are for grown-ups. I know there's a president and that there's like two main teams, red and blue. We learned about how laws are made in school, like a bill becomes a law. I think people should be nice to each other and share. I think it's bad when people are mean. My mom and dad don't talk about politics that much around me, sometimes a little when the news is on. I think I'd want everyone to have enough food and stuff. Is that political?

follow_ups.question: Do you talk about politics at school at all?
follow_ups.response: Not really. We learned about voting and presidents and stuff. We did a mock vote for class president in third grade and I voted for my friend Aanya, she won.

follow_ups.question: What does your family watch for news?
follow_ups.response: My dad watches Fox sometimes in the morning when he's drinking coffee. My mom listens to NPR in the car. I usually just zone out because they talk about boring stuff like the economy.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I don't think I've had any changes because I don't really have views yet. I guess I learned more about how the government works this year, like the three branches, that was new. But that's just school stuff.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: I've heard of it. We talked a little in school about Martin Luther King Jr. and about how things weren't fair a long time ago and still aren't sometimes. I think everyone should be treated the same and it's not okay to be mean to someone because of their skin. My friend Aanya is brown and Caleb is Black and I don't think about it really, they're just my friends.

follow_ups.question: Has anyone ever been mean to your friends because of how they look?
follow_ups.response: Not at our school that I've seen. Mrs. Halverson would not let that happen, she's serious about being kind. But I heard about stuff happening other places on the news.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think they raise that people should be treated fair by the police and everyone. That seems right to me. I don't know a lot of the details though. My mom says it's complicated which usually means I'll understand more when I'm older.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: Just that people are different and that's good. We had a thing at school for Black History Month and I learned about Ruby Bridges and that made me sad and also impressed. I don't know what else to say.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I haven't done anything like a protest. I just try to be nice to everyone at school. I asked my mom some questions about it once after the Ruby Bridges thing and she explained it.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: I don't know really. My parents don't talk about it a lot with me. They just say be kind, treat everyone fair. My grandma sometimes says things that mom says aren't okay but I don't really get it.

follow_ups.question: What kind of things does your grandma say?
follow_ups.response: Um, I don't want to say it. But like old people stuff sometimes. Mom corrects her.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: I'm pretty healthy I think. I get colds sometimes. I have like seasonal allergies and I take a chewable Zyrtec in the spring because the cedar makes my eyes itchy. I've never broken a bone. I had my tonsils out when I was six because I kept getting strep, that was the biggest thing. I wear glasses for reading but not all the time.

follow_ups.question: Tell me about the tonsils thing — do you remember it?
follow_ups.response: Kinda. I remember the popsicle they gave me after, it was red. And I couldn't eat normal food for like a week, just jello and yogurt. My mom let me watch tons of cartoons.

follow_ups.question: What kind of glasses do you have?
follow_ups.response: Blue frames, kinda round. I only wear them for like the board at school or for reading. Otherwise they're in my desk.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: Easy: my mom cooks real food a lot like vegetables and chicken, and I play outside and do soccer so I get exercise. Hard: I really really like sweets and pancakes with lots of syrup, and I would eat mac and cheese every day if I could. Also screens, my mom says I'd stay on Minecraft forever if she let me.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: Nothing big. I had the flu pretty bad last January, I was out of school for a week. And I sprained my ankle in soccer practice last fall but it wasn't broken, just had to ice it and not run for two weeks.

follow_ups.question: How did the ankle sprain happen?
follow_ups.response: I stepped weird in a pothole on the practice field. I cried, I'm not gonna lie. Coach Davis carried me to the bench.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: Not really. The ankle thing meant I missed two soccer games which was annoying. And the flu I missed a science fair planning day. But nothing big.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Yeah, my grandpa with the heart thing I said before. That was scary because we didn't know if he'd be okay. We drove to Tyler a few times to visit him at the hospital. Mom was sad a lot. He's better now though.

follow_ups.question: What was it like seeing him in the hospital?
follow_ups.response: He looked smaller. Like in his bed with the tubes and stuff. But he smiled when he saw us and told me a joke about his TV remote. He's still my Grandpa.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: It's been fine for me. My mom is a nurse so she knows about doctor stuff. We go to the pediatrician in Rockwall for my checkups. I don't know about money or anything for that.

follow_ups.question: Does mom take you to the doctor or dad?
follow_ups.response: Mom always. She knows all the questions to ask. Dad takes me to the dentist sometimes.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Um, my Grandma Joan does essential oils and stuff and she rubs lavender on me sometimes when I have a headache. And my mom has us drink ginger tea when our stomach hurts. Is that alternative? I don't know.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I'm nine, I don't smoke or drink. Gross. My parents drink wine sometimes at dinner, like one glass, but not much.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: Just my Zyrtec for allergies in the spring. And ibuprofen for when my ankle hurt. That's it.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: I think my mom's job has insurance. She talks about it sometimes. I don't really know.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I get my shots. I don't like needles, who does, but my mom says they're important. I had my flu shot in October. I cried a little but only after.

transcript.question_text: What are your trusted sources of information about the vaccine?
transcript.response: My mom. She's a nurse so she knows. And my pediatrician Dr. Nguyen.

transcript.question_text: Now we're going to talk a bit more about what life was like for you over the past year. Tell me all about how you have been feeling.
transcript.response: Mostly good. I'm pretty happy most days. I worry a lot about school stuff, like if I'm gonna get a project done or if I did something wrong. My mom calls me a worrier. I get nervous before tests and before soccer games sometimes. But I'm also like, excited about lots of stuff, like new comics coming out and summer is almost here and I'm doing art camp.

follow_ups.question: What do you do when you're really worried?
follow_ups.response: I usually go draw. Like if I'm stressed I'll just sit and draw and that calms me down. Or I'll tell my mom and she'll talk it through with me. Sometimes I just lay on the floor with Biscuit.

follow_ups.question: Tell me about art camp.
follow_ups.response: It's at the community center for two weeks in July. They do drawing and painting and one day clay. I went last year and made a comic and a clay sloth that's on my windowsill.

transcript.question_text: Tell me a story about a time in the last year when you were in a rough place or struggling emotionally.
transcript.response: When my grandpa was in the hospital, that was rough. I couldn't sleep one night because I was thinking what if he doesn't come home. And I had a science fair project the same week and I felt like everything was too much. I cried in my room and my dad came and we just sat for a while and he said it's okay to be scared.

follow_ups.question: How did the science fair end up going?
follow_ups.response: I got an okay grade. I did a project on why leaves change color. It wasn't my best work but my teacher was understanding.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they struggle with depression, anxiety, or something else like that. How about for you?
transcript.response: My mom says I'm anxious sometimes. Like I get worried about little stuff a lot. She talked about taking me to see a counselor and I went to one once at school to talk about test stress. I don't have like depression I don't think. Just the worry thing.

follow_ups.question: What was it like talking to the school counselor?
follow_ups.response: She was nice. Her name's Ms. Reyes. She taught me a breathing thing where you breathe in for four and out for four. I use it before tests now.

transcript.question_text: How has it been for your family?
transcript.response: Mom's been kinda stressed with grandpa and with her work schedule changing. Dad seems pretty steady. Ellie is too little to be stressed she just wants snacks.

transcript.question_text: Some people say that religion or spirituality is important in their lives, for others not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: Yeah, my family is Christian, Baptist. We go to First Baptist in Royse City every Sunday almost. I do Sunday School. We pray before dinner and at bedtime. I believe in God. I have a kid's Bible with pictures and I read it sometimes. My favorite stories are Noah's Ark and David and Goliath. We do Vacation Bible School in the summer for a week, that's fun, they do crafts.

follow_ups.question: What do you like best about church?
follow_ups.response: The singing actually. We sing songs and there's a band, not just an organ, like guitars too. And Pastor Tim tells funny stories. And the snacks at Sunday School.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever have questions about God or religion?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes. Like why does bad stuff happen if God is good. My mom said it's a question lots of people ask. I'm still figuring it out.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they use Facebook, Instagram, or other social media to stay connected with the wider world. How about for you? Tell me all about how you use these types of platforms.
transcript.response: I don't have social media. My mom says not until I'm thirteen. I do have a YouTube Kids account though and I watch a lot of stuff on there, like Minecraft videos and drawing tutorials. And we have a family Roblox account I share with Ellie. My mom posts pictures of me on Facebook sometimes which I think is annoying.

follow_ups.question: Who are your favorite YouTubers?
follow_ups.response: There's this guy ZHC who draws huge stuff like a giant house and paints it crazy colors. And Aphmau does Minecraft roleplays. And Art for Kids Hub does step by step drawing tutorials.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they use Facebook or Twitter to get (emotional or financial) support during tough times. What about you?
transcript.response: No, I don't use that stuff. I just talk to my mom or Jacob if something's wrong.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your level of stress, worry, and your emotional coping strategies.
transcript.response: Since the school counselor thing I'm better at the breathing trick. And I try to draw more when I'm anxious. School's been kinda stressful with state tests this month but they're almost done.

transcript.question_text: This might be repetitive, but before we go on to the next section, I want to quickly make sure I have this right: who are you living with right now?
transcript.response: My mom Sarah, my dad Mike, my sister Ellie, and Biscuit the dog. That's it.

transcript.question_text: Any babies or small children?
transcript.response: Ellie is five, she's little but not a baby.

transcript.question_text: Anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Any lodgers, boarders, or employees who live here?
transcript.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Who shares the responsibility for the rent, mortgage, or other household expenses?
transcript.response: My mom and dad.

summaries.demographer: Thomas Gatlin is a 9-year-old white, non-Hispanic male born August 14, 2016 in Greenville, TX, who has lived his entire life in Royse City, TX 75189 (Q85–Q89). He resides in a two-parent owner-occupied home with mother Sarah (Bachelor's-prepared registered nurse working at a family-medicine clinic in Rockwall), father Mike (self-employed residential contractor with sub-baccalaureate education), and younger sister Ellie (age 5), plus a dog (Q05, Q11, Q58, Q100–Q107). The household is intact, English-speaking, evangelical Protestant (Baptist), and economically stable enough to own their home, fund a college 529, and finance extracurriculars including piano lessons, soccer league fees, and summer art camp (Q47, Q62, Q83). He is enrolled in 4th grade at Royse City Elementary and is firmly embedded in small-town North Texas civic and religious institutions: school, First Baptist Church, youth soccer league, and regional events like the State Fair (Q21, Q47, Q91).
summaries.behavioral_economist: Thomas displays unusually deliberate consumer-saving behavior for his age: he is forgoing immediate gratification to accumulate $80 for a specific LEGO Bionicle set in a transparent mason-jar commitment device, has reached $47 after five months, and his mother has structured a savings 'match' incentive tied to his upcoming birthday (Q16, Q61). His allowance is a conditional, performance-based contract — $5/week contingent on completing all chores, with documented dock for missed recycling — and he responds to the incentive structure rationally (sticky-note reminders, occasional $4 weeks accepted as a 'slower path' to the goal) (Q16, Q81). Choice-architecture is heavily mediated by his mother (decision-elicitation via Socratic questioning) rather than imposed, which has produced a pattern of mom-anchored deliberation under uncertainty (Q03, Q05). He exhibits loss-aversion behavior in his self-described 'worrier' identity and uses sketching as a substitution good for emotional regulation rather than seeking external rewards (Q43, Q45).
summaries.political_scientist: Thomas is pre-political: he can't yet vote, refuses to identify with a party, and explicitly places himself 'in the middle' when pressed (Q23, Q95, Q96). However, his political socialization environment is heterogeneous and visible to him — father consumes Fox News, mother consumes NPR — and he has internalized this as a household tradition of mediated, non-confrontational exposure rather than partisan alignment (Q24). His civic identity is mediated overwhelmingly through institutional participation rather than ideology: church attendance, school mock elections, polling-place tag-alongs with his mother, and regional traditions like the State Fair (Q21, Q23, Q47). On race, he absorbs a values-frame ('be kind, treat everyone fair') anchored by his mother's correction of an older relative's commentary and by school-based exposure to figures like Ruby Bridges, suggesting an emergent affective egalitarianism without ideological framing (Q26–Q30).
summaries.psychologist: Thomas presents as a temperamentally cautious, internally directed child with an artist's interior life: he is described by his mother and self-describes as a 'worrier,' has been seen by a school counselor for test anxiety, and has internalized a box-breathing technique as a portable coping skill (Q43, Q45). His emotion-regulation strategies are mature for his age — sketching as affect-regulation, physical proximity to his dog Biscuit during distress, and verbal disclosure to his mother — and he showed appropriate grief and rumination during his grandfather's cardiac hospitalization, including a memorable concurrent stress-stack with a science fair deadline that his father defused through co-regulation (Q43–Q45). His identity is consolidated around three pillars: artist (primary, central, and aspirational), family-member (most-valued anchor), and learner (school as 'job') — with a clear coherent narrative voice for a 9-year-old (Q01, Q108, Q109). Cognitively he is verbally fluent, spatially capable (LEGO, Scratch), and shows early metacognitive awareness ('mom says it's complicated, which usually means I'll understand when I'm older'), but he also displays expected developmental opacity around adult-domain topics like finances, taxes, and partisan politics (Q26, Q57, Q75, Q95).
